title: The hypertrophy series: intensity windows and their applications
summary: Introduction to intensity windows: intensity is simply the difficulty of a lift expressed as %1RM or RPE, it is the most underrated programming pillar, and most training should fall between 60 and 95%. He explains how relative intensity rises with fatigue, how deliberately 'wrong' percentages can predict fatigue later in a session, and that you can find working weights by reps without knowing your 1RM.
claims: Intensity, frequency and volume are the three pillars of programming
An intensity window can be a single point like 60% or a range like 60-80%
Percentages and RPE are interchangeable expressions of intensity; I prefer percentages
Intensity is just the difficulty of a lift; screaming, burning or pain are not intensity in the programming sense
Intensity is the most underrated programming variable in bodybuilding; you cannot get big pumping 135 on the bar
Proper intensity selects weights that efficiently damage muscle fibers and saves time; too low and the muscle returns to baseline too easily to be challenged
Cardiovascular or mechanical failure usually signals a bad intensity window: too low, or so high that form breaks down immediately
Train mostly between 60% and 95% of 1RM; the range widens in absolute terms as you get stronger
Avoid 1RMs (above 95%) because they are not worth it for tonnage or injury prevention, and avoid going below 60% because it takes too many reps
Each lift, movement pattern and body part has its own best intensity range, found by experimenting with wide windows first
Relative intensity rises as you fatigue within a session; optimal intensity only exists at the start, which is when strength work belongs
You can deliberately use a lowered training max so an apparent 95% is not a true 95%, to learn a new lift or to pre-program the fatigue of sets placed later in a workout
You do not need to know your 1RM to use intensity windows; find a 12-rep max by adding weight until you fail to get 12
